item.title: How to Play Levia in Silver Age
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|competitive

How to Play Levia in Silver Age

Satiate your hunger with Karol's guide to the returning Shadow Brute!

By Karol Ruszkiewicz

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Levia has shown up as a huge contender this Silver Age season, securing three placements in the Top 8 thanks to the efforts of Jacob Clements, Francesco Giorgio, and Kilian Schellekens. I've scoured through these decklists to find which cards are must-includes and what tech the different players have sprinkled in.

Levia already had some great common and rare cards in the past. Dread Screamer, Boneyard Marauder, Endless Maw, and Graveling Growl have all been incredible at punching through raw damage. However, the way these work, it takes some time to get enough cards into the graveyard, let alone enough 6-power attack action cards to consistently play these out while satisfying Levia's blood debt.

In terms of previous equipment, Hooves of the Shadowbeast has been a monster of a leg piece, being extremely flexible in granting not only an attack go again, but also an action point as long as you have a card to banish. That's it. Banish a 6-power card and you can convert your boots into a clean action point. Beaten Trackers...but better?

More recently, Compendium of Rathe introduced further power cards in the form of Embraforged Gauntlet, Engulfing Shadows, and Pound of Flesh.

On the Brute side, we also received some top-tier pieces of equipment that play really well into Levia's game plan. Buzzard Helm helps fix awkward hands, such as drawing four reds, while also filling up the graveyard to enable the old-school Shadow Brute attacks.

Predatory Plating also offers great defensive value and a precious resource when it matters. And it can matter a lot.

Levia's curve often uses 2-cost cards with go again, meaning two blues are perfect for playing out three of these in a row, often performing her iconic attack for 6, then 6, then 6. However, sometimes you're only able to attack twice, and 4 can be an awkward amount of pitch. This is why we see these lists include Vigorous Smashup in yellow and blue, with some running all six available copies. Vigor and top-deck manipulation are crucial for smoothing out certain turns, especially when combined with the toys Levia just received in Usurp the Shadow Throne...

So what makes Levia so good all of a sudden?

Firstly, it's the new attacks.

Big Bonkers

What's better than some over-rate attacks? A whole lot more over-rate attacks! Not only that, but ones that don't require a busy graveyard to get going.

Feeding Frenzy and Feasting Shadowbeast are all-star attacks that not only match the efficiency of the Monarch attacks, but are also much easier to enable. Their effects are satisfied by any banish, not just their own. This means they make great follow-up cards and can also be enabled by cards like Hex Gauntlet and Cleave the Heavens.

Gates to i'Arathael

Cleave the Heavens isn't just a pretty face. It creates one of the most important components of Levia's toolkit: Gates to i'Arathael, a token that unlocks "free" cards from banish. As the game goes on, you'll have more and more juicy targets for these Gates, allowing you to throw out attacks with unparalleled efficiency.

Being able to convert a single blue into a Feasting Shadowbeast for 8 while satisfying blood debt is incredible, especially in Silver Age. Gates are particularly effective against slower decks that give you time to set up big turns and the space to build a hefty banish zone. I recommend leaning further into setting up Gates with cards like Rites of Nightfall, Countdown to Extinction, and more copies of Cleave the Heavens if your local metagame likes to take it slow.

Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger

The big demon makes his way into Silver Age! Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger offers an amazing package against a wide range of decks. Cards like Goremass Summoning, Beckoning Hunger, and Rumbling Hunger are the main ways to get the demon into the arena, and that is one scary on-hit. If your opponent lets this one through, it can take over the game.

While Gates offer a similar effect, not having to pitch that extra resource and having the effect on tap means you can continue playing free cards from banish, as long as you feed the beast, that is.

Blasmophet's upkeep requires you to continue banishing Shadow cards. Luckily, on your turn you're most likely doing that anyway to satisfy your hero ability. However, it's a bit trickier to do so on your opponent's turn. Some cards fulfill this condition themselves. Cleave the Heavens, Embraforged Gauntlet, and Engulfing Shadows all banish Shadow cards in one form or another.

Some cards also benefit from having a Blasmophet in play. The most played one is Consuming Command, a power play if you have it in your banish zone while controlling a Blasmophet. For 1 resource, you get to attack for 6 with go again, and the best thing is that if you continue to load it with graveyard-banishing effects, you can continue to attack with it. Most lists run only one copy, as that seems to be all you need to get the loop going.

Metagaming

There are a few cards that stood out to me, as they made some lists but not others.

Kilian's build seems the most resilient to fatigue strategies. Including two copies of Howl from Beyond opens up a constant loop of power. You play out the Howl, buff up your attack, then banish it from the graveyard with a Dread Screamer or Boneyard Marauder.

Jacob Clements is a big fan of Agility. Including a Test of Agility and Clash of Agility means that, as long as he can win those clashes, he can make these already incredibly efficient attacks even better by giving them go again. Smashback Alehorn offers even more go again and extra power, making it a great setup card for creating explosive turns.

Another point of contention is whether the lists should run Consuming Lash or Consuming Strength. As a general rule of thumb, I'd say go again is more likely to be useful against slower decks, while the extra +2 power pairs nicely with on-hit attacks like Rumbling Hunger and Beckoning Hunger, especially against aggressive decks that don't want to be defending.

Closing Thoughts

Despite just entering this new metagame, these players have turned up with incredibly tuned decks and a strategy for anything their opponents might throw at them.

I hope you got plenty of useful information on how to pilot Levia, because she is not only a highly competitive deck, but also a delightful puzzle to solve each and every game.

item.title: The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/07/2026
item.description:
Pokémon|finance

The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/07/2026

30th Celebration singles plummet, but the anniversary has produced some unexpected winners.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 7, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

"What's Your Favorite?"

No, that's not a rhetorical question. In fact, it's not a question at all—it's the cycle of promotional cards that were first given away to retail stores and passed out to customers to celebrate the release of Pitch Black a couple of months ago. Most recently, the What's Your Favorite? Mewtwo was released (I personally picked one up while scoring a drop at Target), and with more eyes than ever on Pokémon thanks to the 30th Celebration release, that was all it took to drive attention to—and drive up prices on—this set of cards.

Along with Mewtwo, which is selling today for about $17, this promo cycle also included a trio of cards that all leapt up in price over the weekend:

Giant jump for Primarina, which went from $10 up to a new high of $23. Zarude had a somewhat more muted climb, going from $28 up to $35. Meanwhile, Armarouge started off the most expensive of them all at $30, and after a wild weekend it's up to a $42 Market Price.

There seem to be more chances at Mewtwo on the way, with Best Buy, Gamestop, Barnes & Noble, and even Macy's all getting in on the action (as well as EB Games in Canada). I will say that I was excited to take my five-year-old to the "event" at Target that was supposed to include activities for little kids, and instead it was just a line for the drop. A bit disappointing. But overall, as someone who has been on the front lines for this release, the excitement is not dying down, even if the prices are.

And they are. The average 30th Celebration hit has been dropping like a rock in price over the last week, with the beautiful Mew ex 152 taking a plunge from $150 down to just below $100. Night Pikachu 150 dipped from $90 to $65 and actually fell below the $70 Gengar ex 154, which fell precipitously itself, from over $100.

Speaking of Mewtwo, who would have guessed that the Futuristic Rare printing of the Psychic boss would dip as low as $40? Yet it has, and I think we'll see even more weakness from it as more and more 30th Celebration hits the market. It certainly seems like no amount of product released could sate demand from long lines and campouts happening across the United States, but all that pack cracking will be felt in the prices of the singles. Futuristic Mew has fared only a little better, settling in around $60 after starting the week off at $90.

As for the extreme top end of the set, the RBG Mews? At the top end listings for the Red variant are all in the $5,000 range, with completed sales both below and above that number in the last fortnight. Meanwhile, both the blue and green variants are selling in the $3,500 range. Even among the top end of the top end Mews, it appears there is a pecking order.

This is one of those Pokémon stories that's hard to believe. Gengar Lv.X from the 2009 Arceus release has unsurprisingly always been worth a decent amount of money. Being a mega-popular Pokémon from a relatively dead era of Pokémon sets was good enough to put Lv. X Gengar at $60-80 for most of the past five years.

But Gengar began climbing in Summer 2025, and pretty much hasn't stopped since. It hit $150 this time a year ago, jumped again to $300 at the beginning of the year, and made it all the way to $500 by August. Fast forward another six weeks and the last Near Mint copy of Lv. X Gengar sold for well over $1,000. The new Market Price officially says $680, but make no mistake, these are running right around $1,000 a listing right now on TCGplayer.

Slowking Prime from Undaunted jumped from $70 up to $90 this week, which is the top of a climb that's been building in momentum all year. Slowking has climbed from $30 back at the beginning of the Summer to over $150 for a Near Mint copy today.

Likewise, Garchomp from the 2009 release Supreme Victors has been on a tear recently. It's up from $50 a few months ago, with the most recent Near Mint listing bringing the card's price closer to $100.

The second Jirachi to climb in price in as many weeks, this time it's the Celestial Storm printing of Jirachi Prism Star that is taking a jump in price. The Steel-type Pokémon began the year just under $10, but began to climb several months into 2026 and had reached as high as $15 by the end of the summer. But Jirachi has been on a continued run ever since, and today you're looking at Near Mint copies beginning around $75.

At the top end of Celestial Storm are several cards making their way up slowly, in fact. Rayquaza-GX leads the way in that regard, going from $300 up to over $350 in the last six weeks, while Articuno-GX is up to over $70 and Scizor-GX is now pushing $100 for the first time. These are pretty incremental moves, but given the leap on Jirachi Prism Star, it wouldn't be a shock for any of these to take a more drastic leap in price in the coming weeks.

It's a busy time in the Pokémon world as 30th Celebration works its way into the ever-changing market, and it's a lot of fun to follow—see you next week!

item.title: Everything You Need To Know About Ink Drops in Disney Lorcana
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

Everything You Need To Know About Ink Drops in Disney Lorcana

Deckbuilding will never be the same

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 8, 2026

|

14 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's a very rare thing for a new mechanic to threaten our entire understanding of a trading card game. Once a game moves past the first few booster sets, you tend to find the foundational aspects are baked in and hard to usurp. Disney Lorcana has decided that it doesn't want to play the game that way — anything but. 

Ink drops are about to change the rules of Disney Lorcana and you need to be ready for them. 

If you haven't been following the reveal season leading into Hyperia City, you may not be familiar with what an ink drop is. Ink drops are a new token type that can be created by a menagerie of cards, each of which provides you with a temporary ink. Once you use one it's removed from the game forever. 

This is an absurdly flexible resource. You can stockpile these tokens until it's time to cash in on something huge, accelerate towards a card ahead of time or simply let them fill in for a card you don't want to ink. We saw the power of Sail the Azurite Sea jumping straight to four ink for well over a year and that's the floor on a card like Another Tale to Spin. 

The thing is? That's not all you can do. Hyperia City contains cards that reward you for spending ink drops on them, allowing your new resource to be converted into card draw, additional stats or bonus effects. You'll need to balance these upsides against the power of acceleration and that makes for a wonderful new deckbuilding puzzle. 

I cannot understate how impactful this new mechanic is going to be. Deckbuilding fundamentally changes solely off the existence of ink drops, because you can consistently play on odd numbers/even numbers of ink if you consistently generate ink drops. Mapping out how each color can create ink drops will inform which other cards are playable going forward. This is very emblematic of previous Sapphire deckbuilding to me, but I'm excited to see what it's no longer limited to one color. 

At my count, there are 45 cards in Hyperia City that care about (or create) an ink drop. I want to pinpoint a few of the most impressive ones in each ink and work through what they enable after the release of Hyperia City. 

Amber

We're starting with Amber because it has the least options for ink drops by far. Personally, I think this is deliberate. You can accent Amber with a different ink if you want acceleration, or you can lean into existing tools like Grandmother Willow - Ancient Advisor or Lantern if jumping from two to four is your goal. 

Port Authority - Center Hub is an interesting one. It reads a little awkward to provide the bonus to both players for the work that you're doing, but I haven't forgotten how potent McDuck Manor - Scrooge's Mansion and The Queen's Castle - Mirror Chamber used to be. The stat line on this is very powerful despite it being uninkable.

I'm concerned because it doesn't bridge naturally into Raging Storm, which is the biggest Amber tool I want to accelerate into. If you play Port Authority on turn four, you can move a character into it on turn five to jump to six ink. This only puts you to seven ink on turn six and forces you to have a character in play that'll get swept up by Raging Storm when you play it.

You could play it on turn five and immediately move in a character to fix this? Perhaps you should accelerate into Stitch - Carefree Surfer instead? Unsure. 

In contrast, I think Mickey Mouse - Best in Town is a bit of a beast. It's possible that it fixes the curve issues with Port Authority while providing you with a cheap character to move into it. It may be a hot take, but I think Mickey is much better in a control shell than an aggressive one despite the two lore pips. 

If your opponent is wasting time clearing Mickey, it is buying you the time you want to reach your inevitability. If you're an aggressive deck, you also probably cannot use the ink drops you're generating as well as your opponent. I think there's a lot of power in putting your opponent between a rock and a hard place like this. You either keep questing away... or wreck the opposing counterplay with an opposing Raging Storm. 

Both of these cards have me interested in playing on odds. A Mickey Mouse - Best in Town on turn one allows you to jump to any odd number you like if it's staying alive, while Port Authority is essentially just moving your ink forward a turn. That has me looking at cards like Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty and Cheshire Cat - Inexplicable as other cards that may make for good haymakers. 

Amethyst 

Amethyst gets significantly more ink drop synergies — eight cards, in fact. However, I expect most of the deckbuilding here to revolve around Madam Mim - Resourceful Trickster.

Mim is the payoff. Immediately drawing two cards on play is quite powerful but drawing additional cards every turn you remove an ink drop leads to an obscene snowball. I believe this is an effect worth building around, so I'm looking for other cards that both accelerate to eight cleanly and generate repeatable ink drops. 

Merlin - Profoundly Curious is far-and-away the obvious stalwart here. In a vacuum, the card is powerful enough on its own, threatening to draw cards as it quests and bridge you directly to six. It also enables the Christmasland scenario of shifting into Merlin - Ink Drop Tinkerer to take you to a theoretical nine ink on turn six. 

That means you're jamming Madam Mim and scoring value from both abilities in the same turn with any one cost card. I'm just expecting this card to see a lot of play either way. 

Inkcaster Skates is very interesting to me. It's one of the few repeatable ways to generate ink drops in the game. Assuming you activate it on turn three when playing it, it'll also allow you to reach eight ink on turn five. That's absolutely perfect for Madam Mim! It's not big or flashy, but I think it has some potential. 

I've also seen a few people talking about Higitus Figitus, but I can't say I'm a believer in this one. Six ink is just so much solely jump your ink drop count. I find myself wishing this card had Sing Together, but frankly that may have been a little bit too good. 

Emerald

Emerald also seems to be quite interested in ink drops, with a hefty nine cards that care about the new mechanic. Interestingly, two of these cards were given epic rarity counterparts, each of which direct you into one of the different directions you can take with Emerald. 

You can jump from two to four like a Bollywood version of Sail the Azurite Sea and Tipo - Growing Son, or you can lean into item synergies and jump up to seven. 

Another Tale to Spin and Molly Cunningham - Remembers to Share are the no-questions-asked accelerants on turn two assuming you don't mind offering an ink drop to your opponent. While this will come back to bite you on occasion, I do think you can build your deck in a way to better abuse the acceleration with a high density of four cost characters. 

Shere Khan - Opportunistic Tycoon and Merlin - Profoundly Curious seem like a wonderful fit to continue up the curve, but maybe something like Cinderella - Ballroom Sensation also tickles your fancy. It seems very easy to daisy-chain from two-to-four-to-six. 

Go Go Tomago - Extreme Tester can achieve the similar thing without providing ink to the opponent but requires them to pick her off in a challenge in order to secure your ink. I think this makes her a better fit in an aggressively slanted deck that can punish with a five-cost card if the opponent tries to slow her down more so than a guaranteed accelerant. This is Business and Kit Cloudkicker - Irrepressible Bear might fit into a shell like that nicely as well. 

The other angle of attack seems to be item focused. Baymax - Lab Assistant is a demon if you can consistently activate it, jumping you straight to a seven-ink turn on turn five. That's a magic number for threats like Milo Thatch - Getting His Hands Dirty or Hades - Infernal Schemer. Even if there isn't quite enough in the chamber just yet, I feel like this card is priced to move. 

Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits isn't the set championship promo card by accident. This is a turbo-fixed spin on Hiram Flaversham - Toymaker, one of the only cards to be banned in the history of Lorcana. The math gets a little weird here because you can play items either before or after Honey Lemon to fuel her ability, changing which numbers you'll want to focus on hitting. Cheap items will make you play smoother on odd numbers, which can be a huge boon for a different item payoff like Ariel - Collector of Oddities... but that's less true if you banished a Blinding Chem Ball. Suddenly, you begin to see all the permutations here. 

I think Bobby Zimuruski - Soundboard Whiz is mostly its own little sidequest. Assuming you have one Bobby and one Leaning Tower of Cheese-a, this can be a quite way to jump up on odd numbers too. Maybe that makes it good enough to enable Baymax, too. 

Ruby 

There's something horrific about the implications of Tadashi Hamada - Making Waves needing to be banished to make ink drops. Does he die again in this card? Can we stop wishing ill on poor Tadashi?! 

Ruby falls on the lower side of ink drop compatibility right now with only five tools to choose from. That being said, I think it may have some of the stronger glue pieces in Meilin Lee - Ecstatic Fan, Pushing Boundaries, and Wasabi - Called into Battle. 

Pushing Boundaries isn't that exciting: it's just yet another way to always jump from two to four ink, which is noteworthy alongside those Emerald cards that were looking to do the same. It just happens to scale a little better into the late game to give you some insulation in an otherwise-problematic challenge. 

Tadashi Hamada is a little more interesting. There's not a ton of ways to secure two ink drops in one burst because it's such a huge jump in resources. This one can't really be ignored because it's questing for three and happily crashes into an opposing character to turbocharge your way up to Madam Mim - Resourceful Trickster or Raging Storm. It's not gigantic, but it's worth thinking about. 

In contrast, I really like Wasabi - Called into Battle. If you're jumping up on even numbers, this is a great play to extend your board and not use up your ink drop, keeping that bottom effect active. If you can do that, this almost plays like a fixed Mulan - Elite Archer: a card that was almost good enough several times between Ursula's Return and Azurite Sea. I'm quite excited to explore what this card can do. 

Sapphire

It shouldn't be a huge surprise that the infamous ink acceleration color gets a decent slice of the ink drop pie. There are eight cards worth watching in Sapphire for all your ink drop shenanigans, helmed by the signpost that is Baymax - Amped Up. 

 

Obviously, the intended play pattern here is to generate two ink drops with Baymax - Lab Assistant, then immediately shift into the gigantic 5/8 character that converts future ink drops into permanent ink. Personally, I think this is very good. It might be "worth building around" levels of good, especially since Emerald Sapphire would give you access to Honey Lemon - Testing the Limits alongside Blinding Chem Ball, Prototype Chem Ball and Honey Lemon - Ingenious Researcher to buy them back. This is clearly an intended archetype. 

There are a few other standouts here though. A Dark Age No More is what I expected Sapphire to get: the ol' double acceleration. This card really has me looking at solid six-cost cards that I can punish the opponent with way ahead of schedule. Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan immediately comes to mind, but even the aforementioned Wasabi - Called into Battle might be a good place to go. 

I'm going to try and brute force Powerline - World's Greatest Rock Star again and figure out the rest later. There's a lot to like here and I expect the card to do some work. 

In contrast to his Ruby counterpart, I think I'm going to find myself hating Wasabi - Future Thinker. We have seen boardwide Ward be disturbingly potent in the past, and Ward as a whole is clearly quite good at the moment — that's why Emerald Sapphire Mouse House is performing so admirably. Adding that effect with a dose of resist thanks to a 5/5 two-lore character feels like it has potential. I just won't be the one exploring it! 

Finally, we have to note Intense Research. If you're spending an ink drop on this card, it's just Visions of the Future. That card was a tried-and-true staple during almost its entire tenure in Core Constructed and I expect the same from Intense Research if ink drops are plentiful. You just have to build your deck as to not use your ink drops on other cards. 

Steel

I saved the big one until last. There are an astounding thirteen cards in Steel that interact with ink drops and some of them are absolute haymakers. We'd be remiss if we didn't begin the discussions with the tiger in the room: Shere Khan - Khan Industries CEO. 

This card is a monster. I have it pegged as one of the best in the set. "New Incentive" enables some backbreaking blowouts alongside characters like Cheshire Cat - Inexplicable, and "Corner the Market" will almost always score you an ink drop on the turn Shere Khan is played because of it. 

That means its removal, acceleration and stats all baked into a single card... which is ridiculous. Curving Shere Khan into Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan is going to be disgusting, but you're going to have to get used to it. 

Khan Transport Delivery is yet another means of "sailing" up to four ink on turn three, but it might be the one that's closest to Sail the Azurite Sea on account of replacing itself. I also think Ink Explosion might be a bit of an underappreciated gem in a world with so many ways to jump to four ink. Consider the following: 

  • Turn 1: Mickey Mouse - Best in Town 
  • Turn 2: Khan Transport Delivery. Quest with Mickey
  • Turn 3: Ink Explosion the first answer to Mickey. Quest with Mickey
  • Turn 4: Prince Charming - Protector of the Realm (or frankly any seven-cost character!) 

It's not always going to come up this way, but I do expect Ink Explosion to remove a threat and refund the ink drop you spend on turn three reasonably often, opening up deckbuilding space for five-cost options like Broadway - Sturdy and Strong too. I'm a big fan of the possibilities here! 

I also think that Marie - Caught in the Act might be the most dangerous ink drop generator of them all. The little kitten not only enables ink from turn two onwards with effects like The Terror that Flaps in the Night, but the card will also be online every time a wayward Strength of a Raging Fire stamps out an opposing character. I think sequencing with Marie is going to be very important, but the card is clearly very strong. 

Closing Thoughts

...and breathe! 

That's a healthy chunk of information to process about ink drops and their various cards. Hopefully the eternal whirring of my mind will help your early deckbuilding attempts with ink drops in mind. 

Be sure to let me know how you get on! If you've got further questions, let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From Yu-Gi-Oh's Beyond the Brave
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|finance

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From Yu-Gi-Oh's Beyond the Brave

There's plenty of new staples in Yu-Gi-Oh's newest set (and also, Time Wizard!).

By Zachariah Butler

|

Published Oct 9, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

Beyond the Brave is finally here, and it's a doozy! Angelechy, Light and Darkness Ritual, Destiny HERO and more all gain a ton of great new tricks for their arsenals, and it's going to change the landscape of competition.

While it's not as obviously powerful as Chaos Origins or other sets may be, it's one of those deceptively strong sets that has a lasting impact for quite a while. The YCS in Houston is next weekend, and we'll have to see what it does for the game. Let's dive into the main cards I think everyone has their eyes on, starting with one I'm particularly excited for.

The Cards Everybody Wants From Beyond the Brave

#10 Dark Time Wizard

Board wipes are always in high demand, but when they're given the flexibility of a card like Dark Time Wizard, it's a rare win! Not only is it a board breaker, it's also a tutor for any card that mentions Dark Time Wizard. My personal favorite thing is splashing it into decks alongside Red-Eyes Black Dragon Exceed for even more flexibility. Regardless of which field you break with Dark Time Wizard, you can Special Summon Red-Eyes Exceed Dragon and continue to push through their fields with ease.

#9 Verre, the Maid of Endymion

The final piece of the puzzle for Fairy Tail, Verre, the Maid of Endymion is here at least. This card makes an already surprisingly strong deck even better. The Witchcrafter Fairy Tail deck has been a menace in the OCG for a while now, so being able to play it in the TCG will be a treat!

#8 Destiny HERO – Doom Overlord

Destiny HERO is one of those decks that never truly did much, despite the engine being one of the best examples of the changes the game was going through in its prime. Fast forward to now, and Destiny HERO is finally a real deck! Destiny HERO - Doom Overlord is a fantastic starter, sending any other Destiny HERO from your deck to your grave, but it tutors your Field Spell and when you're going second can be a utility card, banishing an opposing monster. That's amazing design, and I'm curious to see what Destiny HERO can do.

#7 Theorealized Medius

The Ars Magna cards are here, and thanks to Theorealized Medius, the Power Patron and Ars Magna cards fit seamlessly together. Another perfect Normal Summon in a lore theme, we saw how good Fallen of the White Dragon was, so I wouldn't be surprised to see this do that well or even better. A free summon alongside additional consistency for your Theorealize Spell or Trap cards, it'll create a massive impact on the format. In the OCG currently, this card is all the rage, and it's easy to see why.

#6 Angelechy Castellan

Angelechy gets another piece of utility, now gaining removal! Angelechy Castellan really drives home the point that this deck is aiming to play a completely different game than Yu-Gi-Oh itself. Column placement is already important, and we've seen it come up from time to time where people get punished by sloppy play. Infinite Impermanence, Relinquished Anima and cards of that ilk are always around and ready for some skill expression. It's also great for sending your Angelechy cards to the grave, loading you up for even more powerful plays. It also prevents either player from stacking large amounts of effects in a chain, which is incredibly good. Being restricted to one effect per chain is nothing short of back breaking for most decks.  

#5 Dark City at Midnight

We've seen for at least a decade just how good Field Spells are, and now Destiny HERO gets a new one that offers utility going first, going second and on destruction! Being able to tutor any Destiny HERO or card that mentions one by name? That's crazy. If you summon a Level 8 or higher Destiny HERO, your monsters get a nice boost of 300 attack and if your Dark City at Midnight is destroyed, you can summon a Destiny HERO and it's treated as if it were summoned by Clock Tower Prison. This card does so much for the deck!

#4 Ars Magna the Finite and the Infinite

Power Patron was already a deceptively consistent deck, and thanks to Ars Magna the Finite and the Infinite, it's even better! Banishing it from your hand nets you any non-warrior Ars Magna, then your Power Patron Pendulum monsters attack values will all be tripled. If you summon a Fusion or Link monster you can just slam this behemoth back on the field and then if you have a Power Patron Link monster, banish a monster on the field. That's all rolled into 1 card, holy smokes.

#3 Angelechy Strategy Score

This is a terrifyingly good card, and makes Angelechy go from "decent" to "insane"! Tutoring any Angelechy Spell or Trap card is already good. However, getting to return an Angelechy to the Extra Deck and then Special Summon it? Now we're talking. This is a deck that I'm so excited to pilot, and this card is a perfect example of why. The levels of consideration for all the decisions you make is going to be so interesting to watch. I think this is going to be a great challenge for duelists of all skill levels to navigate!

#2 Hey, Space Trunade!

By far one of the best cards in the set, Hey, Space Trunade! offers so much freeform removal that it's going to be a staple to own in no time. You can crack opposing fields with ease, and if the cards being returned don't go to the hand, there's no draws. You can also use it to return bricks from your hand to the deck, which I love. Imagine drawing a Mind Shuffle, returning it to hand, then placing it to the bottom to draw another card, then suddenly your engine cards are all online and you're punching down on your opponent. That's the kind of flexibility this card is offering.  

#1 The Great Gallant Bandit  

 

The card everyone is talking about, The Great Gallant Bandit is the center of tons of discussions all over social media. Many duelists feel it's a staple, and that it favors going first too well by providing protection. Some feel it's a neat card but doesn't do anything too crazy... yet. There are also top duelists saying that while powerful, The Great Gallant Bandit is not well positioned. We will have to see what happens when we get results from Regional Qualifiers and the upcoming YCS!  

There are so many cards in Beyond the Brave that duelists all over are clamoring for it's hard to believe. Blitzclique got a shiny new toy, Light and Darkness Ritual got some new tools for their arsenal, and so many others are getting better than ever. This set isn't one to skip over, that's for sure.

item.title: Top 10 Most Expensive Cards From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|collecting|finance

Top 10 Most Expensive Cards From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

They're no cheaper in the Echoverse.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Oct 9, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Reality Fracture is the penultimate Magic: The Gathering release of the year, and what an absolute banger it is. 

Not only does Reality Fracture bring back the Lorwyn Five, but it really cracks open on how deep an in-universe set can be. There's (Black) Lotus tokens, a pompous Liliana, and even a Chandra who became a cop instead of a hot-headed Pyromancer. There's something for everyone with Reality Fracture, which also extends into opening some serious value.

Top 10 Most Expensive Magic: The Gathering Cards From Reality Fracture

  • Read More: The Most Valuable Cards in Booster Packs Right Now

With Reality Fracture on the shelves and cards starting to enter circulation, I'll be going through some of the expensive hits you can open from the set. Reality Fracture does collectability differently compared to previous set releases, which is to say there's a ton of fancy foil treatments that are worth a surprising amount at present. It's also worth noting there are global distribution challenges with Reality Fracture, which will impact circulation and the value of some of the cards over the next month or so. This is expected to correct itself over time, but this might be why some cards may seem surprisingly expensive.

#10 Ajani Unrelenting (Echoed Pairs Borderless)

Reality Fracture is all about "What If?" and this question cascades into several cards featured in the set, such as Ajani Unrelenting. The Echoverse version tells the sad story about how Ajani didn't fully recover from his brother Jazal's death, making his unrelenting anger into everyone else's problem. In short, he became Magic's version of Kratos.

As for the card, Ajani Unrelenting comes with a slew of interesting abilities serving best in a Superfriends archetype for Commander play. Superfriends is a catch-all term to essentially mean "planeswalker typal", as this means Ajani will create a Cadet token whenever you activate the loyalty ability of a planeswalker you control. If you have enough planeswalkers around, and you'll create an army in no time (how fitting considering the militarian nature of Hexhaven). Then, Ajani can draw you a fresh hand equal to the number of creatures you control and even offers a mini-board wipe that doesn't hit your creature tokens. That's a lot of utility in a six mana planeswalker, and one that's seeing modest value on the secondary market for casual play reasons.

#9 Darklight Phoenix (Shattered Mirror Borderless and Normal)

Snare Thopter returns in Reality Fracture, and appears on one of the more interesting color twists from the set. Darklight Phoenix is a reference to the once-dominant Arclight Phoenix, but this one returns to play if two or more creatures die on the same turn instead. It may be a little hard to get going compared to its predecessor, but it hasn't stopped Modern Constructed players from figuring out the best way to break the card.

At the time of writing, it seems Golgari is the best way to utilize Darklight Phoenix as you have access to Flare of Malice and Warren Soultrader to consistently sacrifice your creatures to return the Phoenix back into play. Interestingly, sacrificing Darklight Phoenix does count itself towards the criteria, making it a little easier to repeatedly bring back again and again. pr

#8 Consign to Memory (Special Guests)

The Special Guests are in Reality Fracture, and this is a small selection of "Masters-style" reprints geared towards the unique collectibility of Magic. Consign to Memory is one of these, and has become a card many competitive players want to open from the set. 

First printed in Modern Horizons 3, Consign to Memory has become a staple of Modern Constructed as it's able to comfortably counter any colorless spell or triggered ability. With Modern currently being dominated by Basking Broodscale Combo and other colorless archetypes such as Eldrazi Tron, Consign to Memory is basically a four-of in most Modern sideboards these days. It does mean the value of this specific printing of the card will remain resilient as there's always a demand from competitive players to snap up nicer treatments of staples for their collection. One thing about the Special Guests is they're becoming rarer to open these days, as these appear in 1 of 55 Play Boosters on average, meaning the more desirable cards will retain their value in the long-term.

#7 Emrakul, the Exigent Doom (Extended Art and Normal)

Speaking of Eldrazi, Emrakul, the Exigent Doom has become a valuable card to open from Reality Fracture, where much of the interest is coming from casual play rather than competitively. Being able to untap all of your lands upon casting the Eldrazi is pretty potent, and one that feels reminiscent of Sword of Feast and Famine or even Prophet of Kruphix in Commander.

One thing I really like about the card is how you can exile Emrakul to essentially turn it into an Ugin's Labyrinth, and then cast the card from exile when you don't need the colorless mana anymore. It's an interesting approach and one that can dodge a Blood Moon if the timing is correct, which admittedly you don't see much in Commander these days. Either way, there's enough going on with Emrakul that I feel it's going to have a place somewhere competitive in the future, just not right now. 

#6 Hexhaven Invigorator (Shattered Mirror Borderless and Normal)

A card that's seen plenty of casual hype since its reveal is Hexhaven Invigorator, which looks to put that many land cards into play under your control equal to the damage it has been dealt. This is another take on Phyrexian Obliterator and the more-forgotten Phyrexian Vindicator from Phyrexia: All Will Be One, where you're looking to maximize as much damage to further your gameplan. 

An aspect that was missed with Hexhaven Invigorator originally is how the card can find any land card and put it into play, which means you aren't limited to just basics. This really opens up opportunities to find a Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle or even a cheeky Maze's End to with through alternative means. Hexhaven Invigorator is a casual player's dream of a card, and its price is holding firm since Primeval Titan is banned in Commander and this is the next best option. 

#5 Eye of Ugin (Special Guests)

Eye of Ugin is another card from the Special Guests that's pretty expensive right now, and this one isn't exclusive to competitive play. While you can't play Eye of Ugin in Modern as it's very much banned, this one still crops up in Legacy and Vintage due to Eldrazi being a known archetype in these formats. However, much of the card's interest comes from Commander as Eldrazi have become an extremely popular creature type to play in the format. With the release of the Eldrazi Unbound Commander Deck from Commander Masters, players are keen to own the nicest version of the Eldrazi cards for their decks — and this stunning version of Eye of Ugin is no exception.

#4 The Theorist, Jace Beleren (Braintwister Showcase and Normal)

Reality Fracture is all about one planeswalker who will do anything but go to therapy, and that's The Theorist, Jace Beleren. That said, opening any copy of the traumatic planeswalker will be a decent hit, and one that's starting to make decent waves in competitive formats. While Jace doesn't have a home quite yet, there's some early success in Standard and Modern Constructed, with the latter appearing in an Azorius Control strategy.

That said, The Theorist, Jace Beleren thrives best in a multiplayer setting due to the passive of drawing a card at the beginning of your opponent's draw step. With the Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck and the popularity of Tam, the Possibility, there's a lot of attention around planeswalker cards that come with a versatile set of abilities coupled with card advantage. Time will tell if this iteration of Jace will dominate competitive play, but secondary market prices are remaining resilient which is a good sign for the card's future.

#3 The Fracture Foil Japan Showcase Cards

The Japan Showcase makes a return in Reality Fracture, with the fracture foils being some of the high-end hits from the release. These are exclusive to Collector Boosters and celebrate Japanese culture for players to appreciate. At the time of publication, the below cards are currently the most valuable from this collection:

  1. The Theorist, Jace Beleren
  2. Emrakul, the Exigent Doom
  3. Kwia Vigorbloom
  4. Ingris Stingerquill
  5. Codie, Ravenous Codex

Unsurprisingly, it's The Theorist, Jace Beleren, Emrakul, the Exigent Doom, and Kwia Vigorbloom that are boasting the most value right now, but opening any fracture foil is going to bring you decent value. What makes this selection of Japan Showcase cards so exciting is the sheer playability of them all. The Theorist is looking quite potent for competitive Constructed, with the Sphinxes becoming some of the best options to play in Commander since the release of Secrets of Strixhaven.

#2 The Facet Foil Shattered Mirror Borderless Cards

Facet foils are a brand new treatment for Reality Fracture, and is perhaps the most striking one yet. These only appear in Collector Boosters and are essentially pseudo serialized, meaning there's approximately 3,000 copies of each of the mythic rare printings and 6,000 of the rare printings. As a result, these will retain some decent secondary market value as they're color bends of iconic cards printed from Magic's vast history. There's 13 of these to collect, with the following being the most expensive currently:

  1. Omnipresence
  2. Hexhaven Invigorator
  3. Darklight Phoenix
  4. Craterclaw Colossus
  5. Return to the Light Realms

Of course, opening any facet foil card will present incredible value just because of how rare they are to open in Collector Boosters. The current prices don't necessarily reflect the playability of the card, as I feel Omnipresence is the weakest out of this collection and expect to drop in price very soon. However, Hexhaven Invigorator, Darklight Phoenix, and Craterclaw Colossus have plenty of Commander and Constructed potential to hold value long-term.

#1 Bloodline Recollector (Serialized, Double-Rainbow Foil)

While there's no confirmed sales of the hyper-rare Bloodline Recollector on TCGplayer at the time of publication, eBay has several listings ranging from $2,500 to $10,000 with the price varying on the serialization of the card. Admittedly, Bloodline Recollector is a bit of an odd choice to have as the headliner for Reality Fracture, but it will remain the most expensive card from the set due to only appearing only in Collector Boosters in extremely low pull rates. 

Compared to Emeritus of Ideation from Secrets of Strixhaven, the Bloodline Recollector takes a little while to really get going as it doesn't enter play prepared. The hoop-jumping to have at least three creatures die in a turn is a lot to ask, and is one that'll probably serve better in multiplayer formats such as Commander compared to Constructed. That said, a black take on Ancestral Recall is plenty exciting, and one that'll influence the card's secondary market price in the months to come.

Magic: The Gathering|finance

Top 10 Best-Selling MTG Cards of the Week - 10/09/2026

Potent reprints at affordable prices.

By Jason Coles

|

Published Oct 9, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Bestselling Cards of the Week

Reality Fracture is finally here, and boy has it been doing well. Prereleases have been jumping, players are building entirely new Commander decks and experimenting in other Constructed formats, and it's just a good time to be a Magic: The Gathering player. How does that all look when checking out the best-selling Magic cards of the week, though? 

Top 10 Best-Selling Magic: The Gathering Cards of the Week - 10/09/2026

That's a very good question, and the answer is below. It's not a huge shock to see it's all about Reality Fracture this week, but we are a little bit surprised by which cards are being bought the most at the moment. Reality Fracture sees a ton of exciting reprints, which is pushing a bunch of sales this week.

#10 Flickering Hound

Flickering Hound is first up, and we're a little bit surprised to see this one first. The card allows you to exile another creature you control and return it to play whenever you cast a creature spell. It's just an excellent good way to leverage more enter the battlefield triggers, and allows for a multitude of value and combo plays in all kinds of decks. 

#9 Path to Exile

Path to Exile is the first of multiple cards from the Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck we'll be discussing today. They're all reprints, which means it's a good time to stock up on copies. This one is a one-mana instant that lets you exile a creature, but the creature's controller gets to fetch up a basic land and put it into play tapped. It's just a really good bit of removal, and it can even be a little bit of ramp in a pinch. 

#8 Multiply By Zero

Multiply By Zero is a really interesting piece of removal. It doesn't destroy or exile creatures, it just invites them to die by giving them a base power and toughness of zero. This is going to mean most creatures die anyway, but it can also be a great way to get around indestructible. The only way this doesn't work is with passive boosts or +1/+1 counters, but it's good nonetheless.

#7 Simulacrum Shaper

Simulacrum Shaper is selling well, and we're not surprised. This card will grab you a basic land card as it enters and then put it into play tapped, it'll also draw you a card when it dies. It's essentially just a more mana-efficient Solemn Simulacrum, but only for green decks. It also happens to be an Elf, which we feel like is excessive, but we're sure the Elf players are happy about that. 

#6 Arcane Signet

Arcane Signet is always hanging around near the top ten best-selling cards at TCGplayer, and it's easy to see why. This two-mana artifact taps for one color in your commander's color identity, and that means it's essential. The Reality Fracture version has some seriously cool art as well, which always helps when you're looking to get a new one for your latest deck. 

#5 Reflecting Pool

Reflecting Pool is a land that can make any color of mana that any other land you control could produce. It's quite strong in Commander, at least as long as it's your second land, and it's a card that is always a popular purchase when it's reprinted. It's also one that comes in untapped, making it an almost essential pick for any deck with more than one color. 

#4 Flawless Maneuver

Flawless Maneuver grants your creatures indestructible for a turn, but you can cast it for no mana if you control a Commander. It's a staple in casual formats, and one of the strongest protection spells in the game at this point. It's also a card that's constantly creeping up in price, so it being reprinted in Reality Fracture is a wonderful chance to pick it up. 

#3 Archfiend of Despair

Archfiend of Despair is the last of the Commander cards on our list. This eight-mana card prevents your opponents from gaining life, and makes everyone else lose life equal to the life they lost during every single end step. It's a terrifying thing to see on the other side of the board in any Commander game, and this was another much-needed reprint. 

#2 Way of the Pyromancer

Way of the Pyromancer is one of the many new ways to augment your planeswalkers. This two-mana enchantment not only lets you Empower Jace 2 as it enters, meaning you get a little Jace token, but also gives your planeswalkers the ability to gain one loyalty to get one red mana. This applies to the Jace token too, which means this is effectively ramps on mana as well. 

#1 Ghalta the Unstoppable

Ghalta the Unstoppable takes the top spot this week because, let's be honest, dinosaurs are cool. Ghalta has been a standout option for green players ever since the first version of the card back in Rivals of Ixalan, and this one is arguably a bit better. At nine-mana, Ghalta has trample and grants your other creatures trample. However, she costs less to cast depending on the power of your other creatures, making it a great addition to any green stompy decks.

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From Yu-Gi-Oh's Beyond the Brave

There's plenty of new staples in Yu-Gi-Oh's newest set (and also, Time Wizard!).

By Zachariah Butler

|

Published Oct 9, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

Beyond the Brave is finally here, and it's a doozy! Angelechy, Light and Darkness Ritual, Destiny HERO and more all gain a ton of great new tricks for their arsenals, and it's going to change the landscape of competition.

While it's not as obviously powerful as Chaos Origins or other sets may be, it's one of those deceptively strong sets that has a lasting impact for quite a while. The YCS in Houston is next weekend, and we'll have to see what it does for the game. Let's dive into the main cards I think everyone has their eyes on, starting with one I'm particularly excited for.

The Cards Everybody Wants From Beyond the Brave

#10 Dark Time Wizard

Board wipes are always in high demand, but when they're given the flexibility of a card like Dark Time Wizard, it's a rare win! Not only is it a board breaker, it's also a tutor for any card that mentions Dark Time Wizard. My personal favorite thing is splashing it into decks alongside Red-Eyes Black Dragon Exceed for even more flexibility. Regardless of which field you break with Dark Time Wizard, you can Special Summon Red-Eyes Exceed Dragon and continue to push through their fields with ease.

#9 Verre, the Maid of Endymion

The final piece of the puzzle for Fairy Tail, Verre, the Maid of Endymion is here at least. This card makes an already surprisingly strong deck even better. The Witchcrafter Fairy Tail deck has been a menace in the OCG for a while now, so being able to play it in the TCG will be a treat!

#8 Destiny HERO – Doom Overlord

Destiny HERO is one of those decks that never truly did much, despite the engine being one of the best examples of the changes the game was going through in its prime. Fast forward to now, and Destiny HERO is finally a real deck! Destiny HERO - Doom Overlord is a fantastic starter, sending any other Destiny HERO from your deck to your grave, but it tutors your Field Spell and when you're going second can be a utility card, banishing an opposing monster. That's amazing design, and I'm curious to see what Destiny HERO can do.

#7 Theorealized Medius

The Ars Magna cards are here, and thanks to Theorealized Medius, the Power Patron and Ars Magna cards fit seamlessly together. Another perfect Normal Summon in a lore theme, we saw how good Fallen of the White Dragon was, so I wouldn't be surprised to see this do that well or even better. A free summon alongside additional consistency for your Theorealize Spell or Trap cards, it'll create a massive impact on the format. In the OCG currently, this card is all the rage, and it's easy to see why.

#6 Angelechy Castellan

Angelechy gets another piece of utility, now gaining removal! Angelechy Castellan really drives home the point that this deck is aiming to play a completely different game than Yu-Gi-Oh itself. Column placement is already important, and we've seen it come up from time to time where people get punished by sloppy play. Infinite Impermanence, Relinquished Anima and cards of that ilk are always around and ready for some skill expression. It's also great for sending your Angelechy cards to the grave, loading you up for even more powerful plays. It also prevents either player from stacking large amounts of effects in a chain, which is incredibly good. Being restricted to one effect per chain is nothing short of back breaking for most decks.  

#5 Dark City at Midnight

We've seen for at least a decade just how good Field Spells are, and now Destiny HERO gets a new one that offers utility going first, going second and on destruction! Being able to tutor any Destiny HERO or card that mentions one by name? That's crazy. If you summon a Level 8 or higher Destiny HERO, your monsters get a nice boost of 300 attack and if your Dark City at Midnight is destroyed, you can summon a Destiny HERO and it's treated as if it were summoned by Clock Tower Prison. This card does so much for the deck!

#4 Ars Magna the Finite and the Infinite

Power Patron was already a deceptively consistent deck, and thanks to Ars Magna the Finite and the Infinite, it's even better! Banishing it from your hand nets you any non-warrior Ars Magna, then your Power Patron Pendulum monsters attack values will all be tripled. If you summon a Fusion or Link monster you can just slam this behemoth back on the field and then if you have a Power Patron Link monster, banish a monster on the field. That's all rolled into 1 card, holy smokes.

#3 Angelechy Strategy Score

This is a terrifyingly good card, and makes Angelechy go from "decent" to "insane"! Tutoring any Angelechy Spell or Trap card is already good. However, getting to return an Angelechy to the Extra Deck and then Special Summon it? Now we're talking. This is a deck that I'm so excited to pilot, and this card is a perfect example of why. The levels of consideration for all the decisions you make is going to be so interesting to watch. I think this is going to be a great challenge for duelists of all skill levels to navigate!

#2 Hey, Space Trunade!

By far one of the best cards in the set, Hey, Space Trunade! offers so much freeform removal that it's going to be a staple to own in no time. You can crack opposing fields with ease, and if the cards being returned don't go to the hand, there's no draws. You can also use it to return bricks from your hand to the deck, which I love. Imagine drawing a Mind Shuffle, returning it to hand, then placing it to the bottom to draw another card, then suddenly your engine cards are all online and you're punching down on your opponent. That's the kind of flexibility this card is offering.  

#1 The Great Gallant Bandit  

 

The card everyone is talking about, The Great Gallant Bandit is the center of tons of discussions all over social media. Many duelists feel it's a staple, and that it favors going first too well by providing protection. Some feel it's a neat card but doesn't do anything too crazy... yet. There are also top duelists saying that while powerful, The Great Gallant Bandit is not well positioned. We will have to see what happens when we get results from Regional Qualifiers and the upcoming YCS!  

There are so many cards in Beyond the Brave that duelists all over are clamoring for it's hard to believe. Blitzclique got a shiny new toy, Light and Darkness Ritual got some new tools for their arsenal, and so many others are getting better than ever. This set isn't one to skip over, that's for sure.
